summary: A country in the northwest of mainland Southeast Asia, formerly called the Union of Burma, known for its many pagodas (such as the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon). It became independent from Britain in 1948, has a diverse population of ethnic groups, and has long experienced internal conflict.

ranking.name: Theravada Buddhism
ranking.description: In 1057 King Anawrahta of the Pagan dynasty brought in Theravada Buddhist scriptures and monks from the Mon and built thousands of pagodas at Bagan, after which Buddhism became central to Bamar kingship and national identity. During the colonial period Buddhist monks took part in the anti-British movement, and after independence Buddhism held an exalted political position; it is a common custom for men to enter the monastery briefly at least once in their lives. Its followers are mainly Bamar, Mon, Shan and Rakhine.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1813 the American Baptist missionary Adoniram Judson arrived in Burma and translated the Bible into Burmese. In the 19th century the Baptists were successful in preaching among mountain minorities such as the Karen, Chin and Kachin, who had originally been animists and had not accepted the Bamar's Buddhism. Christianity thus became a symbol of identity for these peoples and is also linked to their ethnic movements against the Bamar-dominated central government.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the Rakhine and coastal areas in the Middle Ages with Arab, Persian and Indian traders, and during the colonial period large numbers of Indian Muslims also moved into cities such as Yangon. The Rohingya of Rakhine State are the largest Muslim group, but the 1982 Citizenship Law deprived them of citizenship; in 2017 the military's "clearance operations" forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The mountain minorities of Myanmar traditionally believe in animism and ancestor worship, and Bamar Buddhists also commonly worship spirits called "nat"; in the Bagan period King Anawrahta incorporated 37 nats into the Buddhist system. Followers of purely traditional beliefs are mainly in remote mountain areas.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hinduism arrived with laborers, merchants and soldiers who moved in from India during British colonial rule in the 19th–20th centuries, living mainly in cities such as Yangon and Mandalay. After 1962 the military government pursued a policy of Burmanization, and large numbers of Indians were forced to leave, so the number of Hindus fell.

religion.background: The spread of Theravada Buddhism in Myanmar can be traced to the city-states of the Mon and Pyu in the 1st millennium CE. In 1057 King Anawrahta of the Pagan dynasty conquered the Mon kingdom of Thaton, brought back Theravada scriptures and monks, made Theravada Buddhism the state religion, and had thousands of pagodas built at Bagan. Buddhism thereafter became closely bound up with Bamar kingship. From 1824 to 1885 Britain conquered Burma in three Anglo-Burmese wars, and American Baptist missionaries such as Adoniram Judson spread Christianity among minorities such as the Karen, Chin and Kachin. After the military government seized power in 1962 it promoted Buddhist nationalism, and in 2017 the Rohingya Muslims of Rakhine State were subjected to mass violence and expulsion.

ranking.name: Burmese
ranking.description: Burmese is the language of the Bamar and has been the language of the court and Buddhist culture since the Pagan dynasty. It became the official language after independence in 1948, and after 1962 the military government pursued a policy of making Burmese the sole language of instruction, making it the lingua franca of the nation's various peoples. But Myanmar has 135 officially recognized ethnic groups, and many minorities still speak their own languages as their mother tongues.

ranking.name: Shan
ranking.description: Shan belongs to the Tai branch of the Kra–Dai family, is close to Thai and Lao, and is the language of the Shan people. The Shan established a number of Shan states in the 13th–16th centuries and after the 16th century were conquered by Bamar dynasties. Shan is found mainly on the Shan Plateau in the east, and the Shan are also the second-largest ethnic group in Myanmar.

language.history: Burmese belongs to the Tibeto-Burman branch of the Sino-Tibetan family. The Bamar moved south from around present-day Yunnan into the Irrawaddy Valley about the 9th century, replacing the Pyu. The Burmese script derives from the Mon script, which in turn derives from Brahmi-derived scripts of southern India; the earliest surviving Burmese inscription dates to the early 12th century, the Myazedi inscription, which is carved in Pali, Mon, Pyu and Burmese. During British colonial rule (1824–1948) English became the language of administration and higher education. After independence in 1948 Burmese became the national language, and after 1962 the military government's Burmanization policy strengthened Burmese's place in education while minority languages were restricted.

ranking.name: Mohinga (fish noodle soup)
ranking.localName: မုန့်ဟင်းခါး (Mohinga)
ranking.description: Rice vermicelli served with a thick fish soup simmered from catfish, lemongrass, ginger, onion and rice flour, with fritters, boiled egg and banana stem.
ranking.history: Mohinga is regarded as the national dish of Myanmar and is generally thought to have originated in the Mon areas of the lower Irrawaddy, made with the abundant local river fish. In Myanmar it is most often eaten for breakfast, and street vendors sell it from early morning. At Buddhist almsgiving ceremonies held at home or at offerings after funerals, hosts also often cook a large pot of mohinga to feed monks, relatives, friends and neighbors.

ranking.name: Lahpet thoke (tea leaf salad)
ranking.localName: လက်ဖက်သုပ် (Lahpet thoke)
ranking.description: A salad of pickled, fermented tea leaves mixed with fried beans, peanuts, sesame, dried shrimp, garlic and tomato. It has a rich texture with the bitterness of tea leaves and the crunch of nuts.
ranking.history: Myanmar is one of the few countries in the world where tea leaves are eaten as food, and the history of pickled tea (lahpet) dates back to ancient times. In the period of the Burmese kingdoms pickled tea was a symbol of peace: when a dispute arose between two countries or two factions, the two sides sharing pickled tea signified reconciliation. Today it is served to guests at weddings, Buddhist ceremonies and other occasions, and is the core food of Myanmar's culture of hospitality.

ranking.name: Ohn no khao swè (coconut chicken noodles)
ranking.localName: အုန်းနို့ခေါက်ဆွဲ (Ohn no khao swè)
ranking.description: A thick curry soup simmered from chicken and coconut milk, with egg noodles added, served with onion, fried noodles, fish sauce and lemon. It has a rich, sweet flavor and is a common breakfast and lunch in Myanmar.
ranking.history: Ohn no khao swè means "coconut milk noodles" and is generally thought to be related to khao soi, the coconut curry noodles of Chiang Mai in northern Thailand, reflecting the long-standing movement of people and trade between Myanmar and northern Thailand. Coconut milk is very common in the southern coastal regions of Myanmar, and this noodle dish reflects the culinary exchange between Myanmar and its Southeast Asian neighbors. It is often made at Buddhist festivals and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Shan noodles
ranking.localName: ရှမ်းခေါက်ဆွဲ (Shan khauk swè)
ranking.description: Rice noodles or flat rice noodles with a sauce of tomato and chicken or pork, sprinkled with peanuts, pickled vegetables and cilantro. It tastes light and savory and is the everyday staple of Shan State.
ranking.history: Shan noodles originated on the Shan Plateau in eastern Myanmar; the Shan and the Dai of Yunnan, China, belong to the same Tai peoples, and this noodle dish is closely related to the rice noodle dishes of Yunnan. Shan State is one of Myanmar's important rice-producing areas, and rice noodles are the everyday staple of the Shan. Today they are also very popular in big cities such as Yangon and are one of the most representative regional noodle dishes of Myanmar.

ranking.name: Burmese curry
ranking.description: A curry of meat or fish stewed with a large amount of oil, onion, garlic, ginger and spices, with the oil separating on the surface, eaten with white rice. It tastes milder than Indian curry, dominated by the aroma of onion and oil.
ranking.history: Burmese curry was influenced by Indian cuisine; during British colonial rule large numbers of Indian immigrants poured into Myanmar and brought all kinds of curries and spices. But Burmese curry differs from Indian curry in using fewer spices and more onion, garlic and ginger, and in treating the separation of the oil (see pyan, meaning "the oil has come back") as the sign that it is done. A Burmese meal usually has several curries and soups, eaten together with white rice.
